q: What MCDS input Y(LET) table did Wang et al. actually use, and can it be recovered from the authors or reconstructed to make the Table 1 parameters first-principles-reproducible?
basis: The 6 fit parameters + published D10 only self-consistently reproduce when Y_X is treated as a free ~55 DSB/Gy/cell (HSG) or ~51 (V79). McMahon 2017 MCDS gives ~34, and Kukla's fresh MCDS 3.10A gives ~8 at low LET (all order-of-magnitude smaller). No independent MCDS calibration reproduces the paper's D10 --- the ~55 value is unexplained by any published calibration and is nowhere printed in the paper. This is the load-bearing gap that keeps the verdict PARTIAL.
next_steps: (1) Email corresponding author (Junli Li, Tsinghua) to request the MCDS 3.x configuration file and Y(LET), lambda(LET) tables used to produce Table 1 and Figs 2--5. (2) Independently install MCDS 3.10A, replicate Wang's nucleus geometry (HSG 6 Gbp, V79 5.6 Gbp) with matching cluster definitions, and generate Y(LET) for all 5+ ion species used in the paper. (3) Refit the 6 parameters on the 106 PIDE curves using this independent Y(LET) --- if it yields a different Table 1 with similar in-sample R^2, that resolves the ambiguity.

q: Does the model's RBE prediction extrapolate to LET regimes not present in the 106-curve fitting set, or does it merely interpolate within the Furusawa 2000 LET coverage?
basis: The paper fits and evaluates on the same 106 Furusawa curves (in-sample R^2 only). Fig 5 mixed-beam claim (R^2=0.762) is the closest to a generalization test, but mixed beams are still combinations of the same base spectra used in fitting. True out-of-sample RBE at unfit LETs (e.g. very low-LET proton <0.5 keV/um, very high-LET Fe-56 >1000 keV/um, or low-energy alpha at ~150 keV/um cell-relevant Bragg-peak regime) is not reported. Given the model's phenomenological character, extrapolation confidence is unclear.
next_steps: (1) Hold out one ion species at a time from the fit (leave-one-out cross-validation over the 5 ions in PIDE) and measure predictive R^2 on the held-out set. (2) Compare model predictions against non-Furusawa datasets: e.g. Suzuki 2000 (alpha on HSG), Belli 2000 (proton on V79), Weyrather 1999 (C-12 on Chinese hamster). (3) Report cross-dataset RBE prediction R^2 --- a meaningful out-of-sample generalization test that the paper does not perform.

q: Would DSB complexity (fraction of complex/clustered DSBs from MCDS) as a predictor outperform DSB number alone, and does the paper's use of only Y and lambda leave predictive power on the table?
basis: The model uses only Y (DSB/Gy) and lambda (DSBs/track), collapsing all cluster-complexity information to a single scalar per track. MCDS 3.x explicitly outputs cluster-size distributions (P(cluster size k)) which are known from Nikjoo/Goodhead work to matter for lethality: 2+ break clusters are ~4x harder to repair than isolated DSBs. Wang's model absorbs this into the phenomenological zeta and xi parameters --- but never tests whether an explicit complexity term improves fit or generalization.
next_steps: (1) Extend MCDS output to include full cluster-size distributions P(k|LET, ion) for the 5 ion species. (2) Extend the Wang model with an explicit lethality-per-cluster-complexity term N_death_complex = sum_k w_k * (fraction of k-clusters) * Y * D. (3) Refit on PIDE 106 curves; measure whether adding this term improves in-sample R^2 and out-of-sample RBE prediction. Report whether the paper's 6-parameter fit is at the noise floor or leaving explainable variance on the table.

q: Can the model be extended to hypoxic conditions where OER (oxygen enhancement ratio) modifies the DSB yield, and does the phenomenological parameter structure allow a clean OER factorization?
basis: The paper addresses only aerobic clonogenic survival --- no hypoxia treatment. Clinically the OER (oxygen enhancement ratio) is dose-modifying (aerobic dose = OER * hypoxic dose to reach same SF) and LET-dependent (OER decreases from ~3 at low LET to ~1 at very high LET). A mechanistic DSB-based model *should* naturally predict this via reduced Y under hypoxia. Whether Wang's fit parameters (mu_y, zeta, xi, eta) transfer unchanged under a hypoxia-scaled Y, or need refitting, is unknown.
next_steps: (1) Use MCDS's built-in oxygen-fraction parameter to generate Y_hypoxic(LET) for pO2 ~ 0.5%, 2%, 5%, 21%. (2) Predict survival curves at each pO2 with Wang's Table 1 parameters unchanged (only Y changes). (3) Compare against hypoxic-survival datasets (e.g. Furusawa 2000 also has hypoxic conditions; Wouters 1997; Nagasawa 2003). (4) Report whether the paper's aerobic-only fit generalizes to hypoxia --- if yes, this is a significant validation and extension; if no, understand which parameter must be pO2-dependent.

q: Does integrating a full track-structure DSB spectrum (instead of the collapsed lambda scalar) into the Poisson misrepair kernel materially change RBE predictions at low proton LETs relevant to clinical proton therapy (~2-5 keV/um)?
basis: Clinically, proton-therapy RBE variation across the Bragg peak is a live controversy (constant-RBE=1.1 vs variable-RBE models). Wang's model uses lambda = DSBs/track as a single number per LET --- but MCDS actually produces a distribution over track-DSB counts (P(m DSBs | one track at LET L)). Collapsing to a mean lambda may lose predictive power exactly where clinical stakes are highest (proton distal edge, ~5-10 keV/um). Wang's Fig 4 shows RBE predictions primarily in the ion-therapy LET regime, not the sub-10 keV/um proton regime.
next_steps: (1) Modify the model to consume the full P(m DSBs/track | LET) distribution rather than mean lambda, keeping the same Poisson misrepair framework. (2) Compare predictions against proton-specific benchmarks: McNamara 2015, Wedenberg 2013, Rorvik 2018 (all proton-RBE-focused models). (3) Compute predicted RBE at 2, 3, 5, 8 keV/um and compare to Paganetti-compilation clinical data. (4) Report whether track-spectrum-aware Wang matches or improves on the clinical proton-RBE benchmarks --- this is the highest-clinical-value extension.
